strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem—accelerating inference of diffusion transformers (DiTs), which is a key bottleneck for real-world deployment of high-resolution T2I generation.

The training-free nature of RALU is a genuine practical advantage: it can be applied to off-the-shelf pretrained models (FLUX, SD3) without retraining, and is demonstrated to be complementary to caching-based temporal acceleration (Table 3), providing additive gains.

The paper offers a clear and well-motivated analysis of the two distinct artifact types caused by latent upsampling (aliasing near edges vs. noise/timestep mismatch), and maps each to a targeted remedy (region-adaptive early upsampling vs. NT-DM). This diagnosis-to-solution structure is coherent and pedagogically useful.

The NT-DM formulation is technically sound: the derivation in the appendix (Eqs. S1–S9) properly derives the correlated-noise strength (a, b) and the rescheduled timestep s_{k+1}, and the JSD-based distribution matching to preserve the original timestep distribution is a principled way to avoid frequency imbalance.

Experimental evaluation is reasonably broad: two base models (FLUX.1-dev and SD3), multiple speedup levels (4×/7× and 2×/3×), a suite of metrics (FID, NIQE, CLIP-IQA, T2I-CompBench, GenEval), and ablations on NT-DM and upsampling ratio. The reported gains over Bottleneck Sampling are consistent and non-trivial (e.g., FID 28.30 vs 34.48 at 4× on FLUX).

The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with informative figures (Fig. 3 pipeline, Fig. 4 artifact-mitigation breakdown, Fig. 5 qualitative comparisons) and an extensive qualitative appendix including uncurated results to counter cherry-picking concerns.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and partly incremental. The noise-injection/rectified-flow-trajectory reasoning is explicitly acknowledged as inspired by the training-based Pyramidal Flow Matching [21], and the edge-guided region selection is a fairly natural application of Canny edges + top-k patch selection. The main claim to novelty (making it training-free) is valuable but the core mathematical machinery is adapted rather than fundamentally new.

The 'region-adaptive' component is simple (top-k patches with strongest Canny edge signal), and the paper does not deeply analyze failure modes—e.g., what happens when edge detection is unreliable or when semantic content is not edge-dominated (textures, gradients, small objects). The upsampling ratio is essentially a tuned hyperparameter (Fig. 6) with a trade-off against FLOPs, but no principled selection rule is given.

Several key hyperparameters ({h_k}, c) are determined by numerical search minimizing JSD (Eq. S10, Table S1), and the stage boundaries/timesteps (e_1, s_2, e_2, s_3) and upsampling ratio are configuration-specific. This raises reproducibility concerns, as the exact procedure for choosing these values per model/speedup setting is not fully specified in the main text.

The evaluation is limited to text-to-image generation on two flow-matching models. As the authors acknowledge, generalization to score-based/DDIM-style diffusion, video, audio, or 3D modalities is unverified. The claim of being broadly 'training-free' would be stronger with at least one non-flow-matching or non-image demonstration.

The comparison against Bottleneck Sampling [46] and RAS [28]—both concurrent/very recent works—is central to the paper's claims, yet the baselines' configurations are only described in the appendix and it is unclear whether they were tuned as carefully as RALU (e.g., their upsampling ratio/sampling ratio settings). A fair-comparison concern remains.

The VAE-decode-based edge detection requires an extra decoder pass; while the paper argues it is <1% overhead, this couples the method to the VAE and adds non-trivial engineering complexity that may complicate claims of simplicity. There is also no wall-clock analysis of the overhead under different VAE configurations.

No human perceptual study or user preference evaluation is provided; the perceptual claims (preserving structural fidelity, avoiding artifacts) rely on automated metrics and qualitative inspection, which may not fully capture the artifact differences emphasized in the figures.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and under-explored problem: spatial acceleration of Diffusion Transformers, which is complementary to the dominant temporal/caching acceleration line of work and offers quadratic token reduction.

The framework is training-free and demonstrated to be compatible with caching-based temporal acceleration (Table 3), yielding additional speedups (e.g., 4.13×→5.00× and 7.02×→7.94×) with minimal metric degradation, which increases practical utility.

Systematic diagnosis and targeted mitigation of two distinct artifact types caused by latent upsampling — aliasing (edge regions) and noise/timestep mismatch — with clearly framed Remarks and visualizations (Figs. 2–4).

Reasonable theoretical treatment in Appendix A: the correlated-noise injection and the s_{k+1}, a, b closed forms are derived consistently with the rectified-flow trajectory, and NT-DM is posed as an explicit JSD minimization over {h_k} and c.
Consistent quantitative gains across two strong base models (FLUX.1-dev and SD3) at matched speedups, plus ablations on NT-DM (Table 4) and upsampling ratio (Fig. 6) that support the design choices.
Strong qualitative evidence: curated side-by-side comparisons and, importantly, uncurated 96-prompt CC12M samples (Figs. S8–S11) that reduce cherry-picking concerns.
The paper is clearly written, the three-stage pipeline is easy to follow, and limitations/broader-impact are discussed candidly (Sec. D, E).
weaknesses: The headline 'up to 7.0× speed-up' is measured against the 50-step base model; against the closest training-free spatial baseline (Bottleneck Sampling), the gains are modest (e.g., FLUX 7×: 7.02× vs 6.93×; 426.01 vs 431.52 TFLOPs), and some metric deltas (FID/NIQE/CLIP-IQA) are within noise, so the incremental benefit over the strongest baseline is not always compelling.

Baseline coverage is narrow. RAS is only evaluated on SD3, not on FLUX, despite being a natural region-adaptive comparison. Other recent training-free spatial/region-adaptive acceleration methods are not compared.

Novelty is partially incremental: the correlated-noise formulation follows the training-based Pyramidal Flow Matching [21], and the paper itself acknowledges this; the main contribution (NT-DM for the training-free case) is a sensible but bounded extension.

Key hyperparameters for the region-adaptive stage (Canny thresholds, choice of k/top-k ratio, stage timesteps e1/e2, caching ratio 0.4) are either underspecified in the main text or justified only empirically; sensitivity to these values is not thoroughly explored.

Ablation evidence is uneven: Table 4 reports only NIQE/CLIP-IQA/GenEval for the NT-DM study, omitting FID, and Fig. 6 reports only qualitative behavior for the upsampling-ratio trade-off (FLOPs vs. prompt alignment) without corresponding quantitative curves.

The dependence of the method on a decoded-image edge map (via Tweedie estimate + VAE decode + Canny) introduces additional design choices and potential failure modes (e.g., textureless or highly repetitive scenes) that are not stress-tested.

The evaluation is limited to T2I on two flow-matching models; as the authors note, generalization to score-based/DDIM-style samplers and other modalities is untested, which limits the strength of the generality claim.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely underexplored axis — spatial (token-count) acceleration of DiTs — and is training-free, so it can be applied to off-the-shelf FLUX.1-dev and SD3 without retraining. The demonstration that it composes with token-caching temporal accelerators (Table 3, up to 7.94x) is a practically useful property that few acceleration papers can claim.

The problem decomposition is clear and well-motivated: two distinct artifact types (edge aliasing and noise/timestep mismatch) are identified, illustrated in Fig. 2, and each is addressed by a specific mechanism (region-selective early upsampling and NT-DM). This structure makes the paper easy to follow and the design choices traceable to observed failure modes.

The evaluation covers two strong flow-matching DiTs at multiple acceleration levels (2x-7x) with five metrics (FID, NIQE, CLIP-IQA, T2I-CompBench, GenEval) plus FLOPs and measured latency, and the appendix adds uncurated qualitative results on 96 random CC12M prompts (Figs. S8-S11), which is more than many acceleration papers provide.

The NT-DM derivation is given in closed form (Eqs. S1-S9) with tabulated hyperparameters (Table S1), and implementation details for baselines, caching integration, and VAE-decoder overhead are reported, which materially aids reproducibility.

On SD3 the results are reasonably convincing: at 3x, RALU achieves FID 23.29 versus 26.63 for the step-reduced SD3 (9-step) baseline at a comparable FLOP budget, indicating that the method can genuinely beat naive step reduction on at least one model.
weaknesses: The headline contribution — 'region-adaptive' (edge-selective) upsampling — is not actually validated by any controlled ablation. Figure 6 only sweeps the global upsampling ratio (10/30/50%), not the selection criterion. There is no comparison against (a) uniform early upsampling of the same number of patches at the same timestep, or (b) random selection of the same k patches. Since the paper itself states (Remark 1) that early upsampling alone suppresses aliasing, the observed gains could plausibly come entirely from upsampling early rather than from upsampling *edges*. Without this ablation the central claim of the title is unsupported.

The improvement over the compute-matched, step-reduced baseline is marginal and sometimes negative. At 7x, FLUX.1-dev (7 steps) uses 431.45 TFLOPs and obtains FID 27.33, while RALU uses 426.01 TFLOPs and obtains FID 28.68 — i.e., RALU is *worse* on the standard metric at essentially identical cost. Latency is 3.37s vs 3.46s (~2.6%). The 'up to 7.0x speed-up' headline conflates step reduction with the method's contribution; the actual speed-up attributable to RALU relative to simply running FLUX for 7 steps is negligible, and the paper never separates these two effects or discusses the FID shortfall.

Novelty is incremental and partly self-acknowledged. Progressive low-to-high-resolution denoising with correlated-noise injection is essentially cascaded diffusion / Relay Diffusion / Pyramid Flow Matching, and the authors explicitly state the noise injection 'is inspired by the training-based method of [21]' and that their derivation is 'not entirely novel.' The residual novelty (training-free application plus JSD-based schedule matching) is modest, and the paper does not adequately delineate what is new versus what is inherited.

NT-DM is justified by a heuristic proxy: minimizing Jensen-Shannon divergence between the target timestep PDF and the realized sampling PDF. The only supporting ablation (Table 4) shows very small metric differences (NIQE 6.84 vs 6.96, CLIP-IQA 0.684 vs 0.679), reports no FID, and does not test the JSD-minimizing criterion against a simpler alternative (e.g., a single global shifting parameter or uniform rescheduling). The claim that distribution matching is 'critical' is therefore weakly evidenced. Table 4 also marks GenEval with a down-arrow even though higher is better, which is a correctness error in the reported table.

Evaluation gaps that affect interpretability: the FID reference distribution/dataset is never specified anywhere in the paper or appendix, so the FID numbers cannot be interpreted or reproduced; no variance or seed-count is reported for the quantitative tables; and there is no comparison against the practically dominant alternative for inference speed-up, i.e., few-step distilled models (e.g., FLUX-schnell, SD3-Turbo), nor any user study. There is also no analysis of whether the region selection is even correct — Tweedie's estimate at an early timestep is very noisy, and the accuracy of the Canny/top-k mask is never examined.

Related-work treatment and positioning are thin in places. RAS [28] is classified as 'temporal' although it operates by selectively updating *spatial* regions, so the conceptual boundary between RALU and RAS is not as clean as the taxonomy implies. The claim that Bottleneck Sampling [46] is 'the sole existing training-free method for spatial acceleration' is a strong assertion that is not defended, and training-free resolution/scale methods (e.g., HiDiffusion, DemoFusion, ElasticDiffusion) are not discussed.

Several design choices are unexplained and unablated: nearest-neighbor interpolation is used for latent upsampling (why not bilinear/bicubic/learned?), the edge mask appears fixed after one VAE decode (what happens if the early structural estimate is wrong?), and the caching integration (Table 3) degrades FID from 28.68 to 29.55 at 7x while being described as 'minimal degradation.' Figure 3 is dense and difficult to read at print size, and some caption claims overstate the evidence (e.g., Fig. 1's assertion that RALU 'preserves structural fidelity' while the 7x zoom-ins still look visibly blurred).

strengths: Addresses an under-explored but practically important problem: spatial acceleration for Diffusion Transformers via latent upsampling, which is complementary to the more crowded temporal-acceleration literature.

Provides a clear, empirically grounded diagnosis of the two failure modes of naive latent upsampling (aliasing artifacts in high-frequency edge regions and mismatching artifacts from noise-timestep discrepancy), supported by controlled experiments (Figs. 2 and 3) rather than just intuition.

The proposed RALU is training-free and requires no fine-tuning, making it immediately usable on pretrained DiTs (FLUX.1-dev, SD3) — a significant practical advantage over distillation/post-training approaches.

The Noise-Timestep Matching derivation (Eqs. 4–7 and Appendix A.1) is mathematically clean, and the correlated-noise injection with closed-form rescheduling parameters (s_{k+1}, a, b) is a principled, analytically tractable fix rather than an ad hoc heuristic.

Demonstrates genuine complementarity: RALU can be layered on top of temporal acceleration methods (Δ-DiT, ToCa, TaylorSeer) and timestep-distilled models (FLUX.1-schnell, SD3.5L-Turbo) for up to 15.91× speedup with limited quality degradation (Table 2), which substantially broadens its impact.

Experimental coverage is broad: two base models, multiple speedup regimes (2×–7×), five quality/alignment metrics (ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, NIQE, T21-CompBench, GenEval), latency and TFLOPs, plus GPU-memory measurements on two hardware platforms.

Ablations are thorough: edge detection method (Canny vs. gradient kernel, Table S3), fixed vs. adaptive upsampling ratio (Table S4), upsampling operator choice (Table S5), JSD sensitivity (Table 3), and uncurated qualitative samples (Figs. S10–S13) to avoid cherry-picking.

Consistent quantitative wins over the spatial baseline (Bottleneck Sampling) and competitive or better performance vs. temporal baselines at comparable TFLOPs, particularly on ImageReward and CLIP-IQA.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and somewhat compositional: region-adaptive/mixed-resolution sampling, edge-guided patch selection, and noise-corrected upsampling are all individually known ideas (e.g., from U-Net cascaded/region-adaptive sampling and video super-resolution). The contribution is mainly in porting and combining them for flow-matching DiTs, which limits the depth of the technical advance.

On several text-alignment metrics the gains are marginal or negative relative to the base model: e.g., FLUX 5× T21-CompBench 0.626 vs. base 0.634, GenEval 0.652 vs. 0.698; SD3 2× GenEval 0.647 vs. 0.703. The paper emphasizes ImageReward/CLIP-IQA but does not fully discuss this alignment degradation.

Baseline comparisons are not strictly apples-to-apples in speedup: RALU runs at 5.53× while Bottleneck Sampling is 5.24× and TaylorSeer 5.37×; some of the apparent quality advantage may partly reflect the different operating points rather than a strictly better method.

The artifact-ratio metric and JSD-based analysis are largely self-defined; the paper does not establish that these correlate well with human perception, and JSD/artifact ratio trends may implicitly favor the proposed design.

The NT-Matching component is specific to flow-matching architectures, and the paper acknowledges this limitation (Sec. D), but the practical consequence is that the full method is not architecture-agnostic; only the region-adaptive part generalizes.

Edge-region selection adds VAE-decoding and Canny overhead (~2.48 TFLOPs) and requires an extra latent approximation step; while reported as small, the extra complexity and the sensitivity to the top-r hyperparameter (r chosen empirically per setting) are not fully characterized.

The method is evaluated only on image generation; whether the region-adaptive early-upsampling idea transfers to video DiTs, where the spatial acceleration axis interacts with temporal consistency, is untested despite being a natural extension.

There is no direct comparison against a simple 'upsample everything early' baseline at matched compute in the main tables, making it harder to isolate how much of the benefit comes from region adaptivity versus early upsampling per se (though this is partially addressed in supplementary ablations).

strengths: Well-motivated problem and analysis. The paper identifies and quantitatively diagnoses two distinct artifact types in latent upsampling for DiTs: aliasing artifacts concentrated in high-frequency edge regions at late upsampling timesteps (Fig. 2), and distribution-mismatch artifacts caused by non-isotropic covariance and skewed timestamp sampling after upsampling (Fig. 3). The diagnostic plots (edge energy / artifact ratio vs. upsampling timestep; JSD vs. ImageReward) directly motivate the proposed design rather than being post-hoc justification.

The proposed RALU is fully training-free and plug-and-play. The three-stage pipeline (low-resolution denoising, edge-region early upsampling via Canny on a Tweedie-approximated x0 decoded through the VAE, and full-resolution refinement) is a sensible decomposition, and the Noise-Timestamp Matching (NT-Matching) component is derived analytically (Eqs. 4-9, Appendix A) rather than heuristically tuned, with the composite rescheduling parameter delta_k giving closed-form expressions for s_{k+1}, a, and b.

Strong and broad empirical validation. Table 1 compares against multiple temporal acceleration baselines (delta-DiT, ToCa, TeaCache, TaylorSeer) and the only training-free spatial baseline (Bottleneck Sampling) on two large DiTs (FLUX.1-dev, SD3), reporting latency, TFLOPs, and five metrics (ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, NIQE, T21-CompBench, GenEval). RALU consistently improves image fidelity and text alignment at comparable or better speedups (e.g., FLUX 7x: ImageReward 0.999 vs. 0.792/0.660; SD3 3x: 0.798 vs. 0.628/0.059).

Demonstrates genuine complementarity. Table 2 shows RALU composes with temporal acceleration methods (up to 9.03x) and with timestep-distilled models (FLUX.1-schnell, SD3.5L-Turbo, up to 15.91x) with modest quality degradation, which is a practically useful property that many acceleration papers do not establish.

Good ablation coverage and reproducibility signals. Appendix C ablates edge detection in image vs. latent space (Table S3), fixed vs. adaptive upsampling ratio (Table S4), upsampling kernel (Table S5), and the JSD/NT-Matching effect (Table 3). Hyperparameters (N, e, h, c) are tabulated in Table S1, baseline configurations are detailed in B.2, and uncurated qualitative results (Figs. S10-S13) are provided, which reduces cherry-picking concerns.

The limitations section is honest and specific (NT-Matching tailored to flow-matching DiTs; no validation on U-Net backbones), and the broader-impact discussion notes both efficiency benefits and misuse risk.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate. The individual ingredients — cascaded/multi-resolution sampling, edge-guided selective upsampling, and noise/timestamp rescheduling — are each related to prior work (Pyramidal Flow, Latent-SR, Bottleneck Sampling, RelaDiffusion). The contribution is primarily in the combination plus the analytical NT-Matching derivation, which is valuable but incremental relative to the framing of 'investigating spatial acceleration.'

Evaluation is restricted to text-to-image generation on two flow-matching DiT families (FLUX.1-dev, SD3). No video, audio, or other conditional modalities are tested despite the introduction citing them; the claimed generality of RALU beyond flow-matching DiTs is explicitly left unverified in Section D, which limits the strength of the 'general framework' claim.

Spatial acceleration is compared against only one training-free baseline (Bottleneck Sampling). The paper argues this is the only existing training-free spatially accelerated method, but a comparison against a training-based spatial method (e.g., a cascaded framework) or an ablation isolating the effect of early vs. late upsampling in a controlled setting would strengthen the claim that RALU is the best spatial trade-off.

The 'artifact ratio' and 'edge energy' metrics used to motivate the core findings (Figs. 2, 3, 7) are self-defined (Canny-based) and may not perfectly correlate with perceptual quality. The paper does partially validate them via ImageReward correlation (Fig. 3b), but a human study or a more standard artifact metric would strengthen the central empirical claim.

The NT-Matching parameters {h_k} and c are obtained by minimizing JSD via numerical search (Table S1). While the search is done once per configuration and thus remains 'training-free' in the usual sense, the resulting parameter set is model- and speedup-specific, and the paper does not fully characterize how sensitive the method is to this choice or how it would generalize to new DiT architectures without re-searching.

The reported speedups in latency (e.g., FLUX 5x: 5.04s vs. 5.37s for Bottleneck) are real but the margin over the closest spatial baseline is modest, and the abstract's headline '7.0x on FLUX' relies on TFLOPs reduction rather than wall-clock, which should be interpreted carefully since VAE decoding and Canny edge detection add non-trivial fixed overhead.

Some presentation issues: the main text defers a substantial amount of derivation and setup (Eqs. S1-S12, baseline configurations) to the appendix, and several figures (Fig. 4, Fig. 5) are dense and would benefit from clearer captions for the artifact-type color coding.

strengths: Targets a genuinely underexplored axis: training-free *spatial* acceleration of DiTs, complementary to the dominant temporal-acceleration line, and demonstrates composability with caching/forecasting methods and timestep-distilled models (up to 15.91× in combination, Table 2).

Provides a clear, empirically grounded characterization of two failure modes of naive latent upsampling — aliasing from late upsampling (Fig. 2, edge-energy/artifact-ratio over 100 images) and distribution mismatch from noise/timestep discrepancy (Fig. 3, JSD vs. artifact ratio) — with an analytical treatment of the upsampled covariance and the correlated-noise injection/timestep rescheduling (Eqs. 2–7, S1–S11) that is internally consistent (a·e_k = s_{k+1}, b = 1−s_{k+1}, a(1−e_k)=b√c all check out).

Within the standard protocol (speedup measured relative to the full-step base model), RALU is the best training-free method at each operating point in Table 1: on FLUX 5× it beats Δ-DiT, ToCa, TeaCache, TaylorSeer and Bottleneck Sampling on ImageReward, CLIP-IQA and NIQE at the lowest FLOPs/latency, and the same holds at 7× and on SD3 2×/3×; improvements on SD3 2× (ImageReward 0.890→0.971) and FLUX 7× (0.792→0.999) over the spatial baseline are non-trivial.

Reasonable and fairly complete ablation suite: edge detection in image vs. latent space, fixed vs. adaptive top-r ratio, upsampling operator choice, JSD vs. downstream quality (Table 3), and the upsampling-ratio trade-off (Fig. 8), plus uncurated 48-image grids and a stated limitations section.

Reproducibility effort is above average for this genre: per-baseline hyperparameters and per-setting stage schedules are listed in the appendix, the metric definitions and evaluation sets (5k MS-COCO images) are specified, and both quantitative and extensive qualitative comparisons are given.
weaknesses: The acceleration actually attributable to the spatial component is marginal, contradicting the paper's framing. Compared against the step-reduced baselines with identical NFE (FLUX(10), FLUX(7), SD3(14), SD3(9)), RALU reduces FLOPs by only ~11.4%, ~1.3%, ~1.2% and ~5.3% respectively, and latency by ~3–5% (5.18→5.04 s; 3.79→3.75 s; 2.14→2.04 s; 1.46→1.38 s). Hence the headline '5.53×/7.02×/3.02×' is essentially the trivial NFE reduction (4.90×/6.93×/2.86×), not the contribution. At 7× and SD3 2× the method is speed-neutral with respect to a baseline that requires none of the proposed machinery. The paper claims resolution transitions give a 'quadratic reduction in computation'; its own FLOPs measurements do not support this, and the discrepancy is never explained.

Technical novelty is incremental. Noise reinjection plus timestep rescheduling across resolution stages is the core mechanism of Relay Diffusion [54] and Pyramid Flow [24] (both training-based), and Bottleneck Sampling [55] already performs training-free spatial acceleration with noise reintroduction and scheduler reshifting. RALU's additions — selecting top-r edge patches for early upsampling and JSD-optimized truncated-PDF timestep matching — are sensible engineering but not a conceptual advance; the paper itself states the noise-injection step 'modifies the approach from [24]'.

Evaluation/reporting is thin on statistical support for the headline claims. Latencies are single measurements with no variance, no repeated runs, and no significance tests on the differences that matter most (e.g., RALU 5.53× vs. TaylorSeer 5.37× or Bottleneck 5.24×; SD3 1.94× vs. 1.92×). The 'Speedup' column is FLOPs-ratio, not wall-clock (FLUX 5.53× FLOPs corresponds to 4.98× measured latency), which systematically overstates the practical gain; the artifact-ratio metric is bespoke and unvalidated against human judgement, and no human study is provided despite the central claim of 'artifact-free' perceptual quality.

Experimental specification contains inconsistencies that impede verification. The stage step counts in the appendix (e.g., [4,16,21] for Bottleneck Sampling at FLUX 5×, [6,24,31] for SD3 2×, and [4,9,15]/[2,5,10]/[5,11,20]/[3,6,12] for RALU) exceed the stated NFE (10, 7, 14, 9) and are hard to reconcile with the reported FLOPs, so a reader cannot determine how much compute is actually executed at low resolution — the crux of the spatial-acceleration claim.

Hyperparameter dependence undercuts the 'training-free' convenience. c and {h_k} are obtained by numerically searching a JSD minimum for each model/speedup configuration (Table S1), and the values finally adopted differ from those returned by Eq. (S12) without explanation; each new base model or speedup factor therefore requires its own optimization, and it is unclear how sensitive the results are to these choices.

The main tables isolate only one spatial baseline (Bottleneck Sampling). The individual contributions of the two key components (edge-selective early upsampling; NT-Matching) are not cleanly ablated in the main comparison — naive upsampling and the no-NT-Matching variants appear only in Fig. 7/supplement — and there is no comparison to straightforward alternatives such as uniform (non-edge-selective) early upsampling at matched FLOPs, or to low-resolution-then-refine schedules without noise injection.
